lesson.title: The Box Problem: Why Cutting 2-Inch Corners Wins
lesson.summary: Fold an open top box out of a flat square of cardboard by cutting equal squares from each corner, and verify by hand that a very specific cut size maximizes the volume.
lesson.body:
The box problem is one of the oldest optimization problems taught in calculus because it is easy to picture and hard to guess the answer to by intuition alone. It also builds directly on the general strategy from maximizing volume: define a single variable, express volume in terms of it, then verify a critical point is really the maximum and not just an arithmetic result.

Take a square sheet of cardboard with side length 12 inches. Cut a small square of side length x from each of the four corners, then fold up the four resulting flaps to form an open top box. The base of the box is a square with side length (12 - 2x), because two corner cuts, one from each end, are removed from every original 12 inch edge, and the height of the box is x, since that is how far each flap folds up. The volume is V(x) = x(12 - 2x)^2, and the practical domain is 0 < x < 6, since x cannot be zero or negative (no box would form) and cannot reach 6 or beyond (the base side length 12 - 2x would hit zero or go negative).

Expand the volume function: (12 - 2x)^2 = 144 - 48x + 4x^2, so V(x) = 144x - 48x^2 + 4x^3. Differentiate: V'(x) = 144 - 96x + 12x^2. Factor out 12: V'(x) = 12(x^2 - 8x + 12) = 12(x - 2)(x - 6). Setting V'(x) = 0 gives two candidates, x = 2 and x = 6.

Here is exactly where verification matters. x = 6 sits on the boundary of the domain, not inside it, and plugging it in gives a base side length of 12 - 12 = 0, a degenerate box with zero volume, so it can be discarded on physical grounds alone. That leaves x = 2 as the only interior critical point. Check it with the Second Derivative Test: V''(x) = -96 + 24x, so V''(2) = -96 + 48 = -48, which is negative, confirming x = 2 is a local maximum. Since the only other candidate is the degenerate endpoint, x = 2 is the global maximum on the open interval.

The maximum volume is V(2) = 2(12 - 4)^2 = 2(64) = 128 cubic inches. As a check on the endpoints of the domain, V approaches 0 as x approaches either 0 or 6 from inside the interval, which makes sense: a vanishingly small cut folds almost no height, and a cut approaching 6 leaves almost no base, and both extremes squeeze the volume toward zero, exactly what pushes the true maximum into the interior at x = 2.

There is a tidy general pattern hiding here. For a square sheet of side length s, the same steps give V(x) = x(s - 2x)^2, and differentiating produces V'(x) = (s - 2x)(s - 6x), so the interior critical point is always at x = s/6 (the other root, x = s/2, is the degenerate boundary case). For our 12 inch sheet, s/6 = 2, exactly matching what we found by direct computation.
